Evaluator: withheld

Condition: MID

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
I want to tell you about light.

Not the grand, cinematic kind of light — not sunrise over the Grand Canyon or the aurora rippling over a frozen lake, though those are magnificent — but the ordinary light that lives in your house without you ever really asking it to be there.

Take the light in the late afternoon, the hour that photographers call golden but that most of us just call four-thirty. It comes in sideways. It has to work to get in, angling past buildings and trees and curtains, and by the time it reaches your kitchen it is tired and warm and amber-colored. It lands on the countertop and makes dust visible. We normally think of dust as a failure of cleaning, but in that light it looks like weather. Like a small, slow snowstorm happening only in your kitchen, only for you.

I think about that light a lot because it is patient. It does not demand that you look at it. It will be there whether you notice it or not, and then it will be gone. If you happen to look up from washing dishes and see it painting the side of the toaster gold, you get a gift you didn't earn. If you don't, nothing is lost. It tried.

There used to be a library near my childhood home that had that kind of light. It was a brick building from the 1960s, not beautiful in any deliberate way, with heavy doors that sighed when you pulled them. Inside, the carpet was the kind of green that hides stains and the air always smelled faintly of paper and radiator heat and someone's old coffee. I went there not because I was a particularly studious child, but because my parents had discovered that the library was air-conditioned in the summer and free, which are the two great virtues for parents in July.

The library had a section in the back, near the large windows that looked out onto an alley and a parking lot, where nobody really went. That was the 900s. Dewey Decimal 900s: history and geography. Other kids wanted the 600s for how things worked, or the fiction shelves where the spines were bright and promising. But I liked the 900s because no one was ever there to tell me to be quiet or to hurry up. The books there were heavy and serious with photographs of places I had never seen and would never see: terraces carved into mountains in Peru, streets in Tokyo lit with signs I couldn't read, the inside of a salt mine in Poland where everything, walls and chandeliers and altars, was made of salt.

I would pull down a book so large it required both arms and open it in a patch of that sideways light coming through the high windows. And I would travel. Not in the way travel brochures mean travel, but in the deeper way a child travels, which is to completely and instantly believe that the world contains salt cathedrals and that this is a reasonable thing for a world to contain.

One day the librarian, Mrs. Sato, found me there. She was a small woman with short gray hair and glasses that hung from a chain. She did not ask what I was doing or tell me to put the book back. She just said, "That one has the best pictures of Iceland. But if you like salt, wait until you see page 88 of this one." And she handed me another, even heavier book. I remember feeling shocked that an adult knew exactly what I had been looking for before I knew I was looking for it.

That is, I think, the highest form of attention: to see someone's obscure interest and feed it without making it feel small.

Mrs. Sato retired years ago. The library was renovated into something brighter and more open, with collaborative workspaces and a coffee bar and excellent lighting that is the same at every hour. It's better in every measurable way. More people use it now. I am glad. But sometimes I miss those dim, dusty 900s and the way the light had to fight to get in.

We talk a lot about big ideas — purpose and legacy and happiness and success — as if they are mountains we are supposed to climb. But most of life is not on the mountain. Most of life is in the kitchen at four-thirty. It's in the library after school. It's in small, unremarkable moments that only become remarkable later when you realize they were shaping you all along.

I have come to believe that our lives are not written by the huge decisions we agonize over for weeks, though those matter too. Our lives are written by the small choices we make without thinking. Whether you look up when the light hits the toaster. Whether you sit in the empty aisle. Whether you hand the strange kid the book about salt.

There's a concept in Japanese called "komorebi" — sunlight filtering through leaves, the dappled light that moves. There's no direct English equivalent, which tells you something about what a culture notices. English has plenty of words for types of rain and for grief, but we had to borrow a word for that particular, dancing light. We notice what we name, and we name what we notice. It's a loop.

I wonder what words we are missing right now. What experiences we are all having but not talking about because we haven't agreed to see them. The specific loneliness of seeing your friends online but not in person. The particular joy of finding a perfect stick. The quiet pride of keeping a houseplant alive for more than a year. These are human universals as true as love or anger, but they live in the corners of language.

A few years ago I started keeping a notebook, not a diary exactly, but a log of small lights. Nothing profound. Entries like: "May 3rd — The way the rain smelled after it hit the hot pavement, like earth waking up." Or: "September 19th — Kid on the bus offering half his cookie to the woman next to him, even though she said no thanks, he kept holding it out for three stops just in case." Or: "November — Found an old grocery list in a used book: eggs, bread, soap, bird seed. Wonder who needed bird seed."

It sounds sentimental when I describe it, but doing it has changed how I move through the world. When you know you are going to write something down, you start looking for it. And when you start looking for it, you find it everywhere. The world is absolutely saturated with small kindnesses and strange beauties if you attend to them. It doesn't mean the hard, terrible things aren't real. They are. But they are not the whole picture. They were never the whole picture.

My favorite entry is still very short. From last February: "The man repairing the sidewalk in the snow. He smiled at me like we were both in on the same joke."

I have no idea what the joke was. But I smiled back.

If you had seen us, two strangers smiling in the cold for no reason, you might have thought nothing happened. And in a plot-driven sense, nothing did. No one was transformed. No lesson was learned. But that smile stayed with me for the whole day. It was a little light coming in sideways. Tired and warm and amber. Arriving whether I noticed it or not.

I think that's what I want to say, if I have any wisdom at all after all these words: Notice it when you can. Look up from the dishes. Sit for a minute in the dusty aisle. Accept the book someone hands you about salt mines, even if you didn't know you liked salt mines. Write down the small things.

There will be plenty of grand, cinematic light in your life too — graduations and weddings and births and that one perfect trip where everything went right. You won't need help noticing those. They announce themselves with trumpets.

It's the other light you need to watch for. The quiet one. The one that falls on ordinary things and makes them, just for a moment, look like weather.

Keep an eye out for it. It's looking for you too.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical personal essay turns ordinary light, a childhood library, and small acts of attention into a sustained reflection on noticing.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, reflective, and gently invitational. Its pathos comes from the tender particulars—the tired afternoon light, the dusty history shelves, Mrs. Sato’s recognition of an obscure interest, and the stranger’s smile—rather than from dramatic loss or triumph. The narrator invites the reader to practice attention without treating it as a cure for hardship: small beauties and kindnesses matter, while “the hard, terrible things” remain real.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly returns to light as a metaphor for unnoticed gifts, linking it to dust, books, weather, language, and everyday encounters. It foregrounds quiet attention and unshowy kindness: an adult nourishing a child’s curiosity, someone offering a cookie, and two strangers smiling in the snow. Its moral claim is that small, apparently inconsequential moments help shape a life, and that noticing them is a practice.

## Evidence line
> That is, I think, the highest form of attention: to see someone's obscure interest and feed it without making it feel small.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the recurring light motif, specific remembered scenes, and consistent invitation to notice small kindnesses make this a distinctive, coherent sample.
